title: Builder and Prototype
goal: By the end you can choose between named arguments, a Java record plus builder, and a Kotlin DSL builder, and make copies of templates that never share mutable state with the original.

warmup.q: `data class Cart(val id: String, val skus: MutableList<String>)`. You run `val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2")` and then `c2.skus += "sku-2"`. What happens to `c1.skus`?
options: It now contains `sku-2` too, because both carts share one list
It throws, because data class properties are immutable
It depends on whether `c1` was declared with `val`
warmup.why: `copy()` is shallow. It copies the reference to the list, not the list, so `c1` and `c2` hold the same `MutableList`. `val` only stops you from pointing the property at another list; it says nothing about the list's contents. Records in Java behave the same way.

sections.h: Prototype: every copy is shallow until you make it deep
sections.body:
Prototype means making a new object by copying an existing one and changing a few fields. Payment code does this constantly: a recurring-charge template copied per merchant, a default config copied per tenant, a test fixture copied per test.

Java's original mechanism, `Cloneable`, is broken by design. The interface has no `clone` method, so implementing it gives callers nothing to call. `Object.clone()` is protected and makes a shallow copy. To use it you override `clone`, call `super.clone()`, catch a `CloneNotSupportedException` that can't happen, and then fix every mutable field by hand. Skip it. Use a copy constructor, a static copy factory, or a wither on a record.

Records make withers easy to write and Kotlin data classes generate `copy()`. Neither copies deeply. The Kotlin docs say it plainly: `copy()` creates a shallow copy, and references to other objects are shared.

```kotlin
data class Cart(val id: String, val skus: MutableList<String>)
val c1 = Cart("c1", mutableListOf("sku-1"))
val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2")
c2.skus += "sku-2"          // c1.skus is now [sku-1, sku-2]
```

```java
record Cart(String id, List<String> skus) {
    Cart withId(String newId) { return new Cart(newId, skus); }   // a wither: shares the list
}
var c1 = new Cart("c1", new ArrayList<>(List.of("sku-1")));
var c2 = c1.withId("c2");
c2.skus().add("sku-2");     // c1.skus() is now [sku-1, sku-2]
```

The fix is the same in both languages. Store collections you can't change (`List.copyOf` in a compact constructor in Java; a read-only `List` in Kotlin), and let withers build a new collection: `copy(skus = skus + "sku-2")`.

Kotlin has a second trap. `data class Email private constructor(val value: String)` still gets a public `copy()`, so `Email.of("anna@example.com").copy(value = "not-an-email")` compiles and skips your factory. Kotlin 2.4 only warns, and the warning says it becomes an error in language version 2.5. Add `@ConsistentCopyVisibility` to make `copy()` as private as the constructor in the current release. Validation in an `init` block is safer still, because `copy()` runs it. Java records never had the private-constructor illusion: a record's canonical constructor can't be less visible than the record, so the rules belong in the compact constructor from the start.

try.expect: It prints `c1.skus after changing c2: [sku-1, sku-2]` (the copy shared the list), `copy() skipped the factory: Email(value=not-an-email)`, and `negative amount: -1`, because `init` runs on `copy()`. The compiler warns that the non-public primary constructor is exposed via `copy()`. With `@ConsistentCopyVisibility`, the build stops with `Cannot access 'fun copy(value: String = ...): Email': it is private`. The Java twin prints the same story: the wither shares the list, `new Email("not-an-email")` skips the factory, and the compact constructor rejects `-1`.

analogy: A builder is an order form at a card-printing desk: you tick the boxes you care about, leave the rest at their defaults, and the clerk checks the whole form before printing anything. Kotlin's named arguments are a form so short you fill it in at the counter. Prototype is photocopying a filled-in form and changing two fields. The analogy breaks on the shallow copy: a photocopy is a real, separate piece of paper, while `copy()` gives you a new form that still points at the same attached sheet of line items, so writing on the copy's attachment writes on the original's.
in_your_world: Payment requests to an issuer have a dozen optional fields: descriptor, 3-D Secure data, metadata, capture mode, retry policy. In Kotlin services, a data class with defaults and an `init` block is all you need. For a shared client library that Java services call, add a builder. Test fixtures are prototypes: one `baseAuthorization` copied per test with `copy(amountMinor = 0)`. If that fixture holds a `MutableList` of line items, one test can poison every test after it. The same goes for a Quarkus `@ApplicationScoped` bean that hands out a default config object which callers then copy and modify.
mistake: The most common mistake is trusting `copy()` or a record wither to make an independent object when a component is mutable. A `MutableList`, a `HashMap`, an array or a mutable `Date` is shared between the original and the copy, so changing one changes both. It happens because the class looks immutable: every property is `val`, or it's a record. The fix is to store copies that can't change (`List.copyOf` in a compact constructor, read-only types and `toList()` in Kotlin), and to make withers build new collections instead of mutating the shared one.

compare.title: A prototype that copies safely

java.title: TenantConfig.java

kotlin.title: TenantConfig.kt
kotlin.src:
data class TenantConfig(
    val tenantId: String,
    val paymentMethods: List<String>,          // read-only types
    val dailyLimits: Map<String, Long>,
)

val base = TenantConfig("default", listOf("CARD"), mapOf("CARD" to 500_000L))
val acme = base.copy(
    tenantId = "acme",
    paymentMethods = base.paymentMethods + "SEPA",  // + builds a new list
)

compare.note: Kotlin generates `copy()` with named arguments, so it needs no withers, and `+` on a read-only `List` or `Map` returns a new collection. Java needs one hand-written wither per field. Both copies are shallow, and the safety comes from the components, not from the copy. There is one real difference: Java's compact constructor can replace the incoming list with `List.copyOf`, while a Kotlin data class property can't be reassigned in `init`. A Kotlin `List` parameter is only read-only, so a caller who passes a `MutableList` and keeps a reference can still change it. If that matters, take the list as a plain constructor parameter and store `toList()` in a property.

worked.title: From a telescoping constructor to a record and builder, and to a Kotlin class

steps.say: Here is a call to an issuer charge request with eight positional arguments. Before reading on, say which argument is the statement descriptor, and which rule you'd expect `ChargeRequest` to enforce.

Put every rule in one place that all paths go through: the record's compact constructor in Java, the `init` block in Kotlin. The cross-field rule (a descriptor only on captured charges, and 22 characters at most) can only be checked where all fields are known. Kotlin also gets its defaults here, which is half of what a builder does.

Java needs a builder that only collects and supplies defaults; its `build()` calls the canonical constructor, so the rules run there. Kotlin needs no builder: named arguments do the job, and `@JvmOverloads` gives Java callers some overloads. If Java teams call the Kotlin class often, add a builder for them too.

lab.title: A validating payment DSL, and a prototype that stops leaking
steps: Run the tests. Twelve of thirteen fail: the DSL is all `TODO`, and `ChargeTemplate` leaks tags and metadata between copies.
In `PaymentRequestDsl.kt`, write `LineItemsBuilder`: keep a private `MutableList`, and return `toList()` from `build()`.

Write `PaymentRequestBuilder`: `lineItems` runs the block on a fresh `LineItemsBuilder` and keeps its items; `metadata` puts into a private map; `build()` validates with `require` and copies the collections into the `PaymentRequest`. Then write `paymentRequest`.
Fix `ChargeTemplate.java`: add a compact constructor that stores `List.copyOf` and `Map.copyOf`, and make the withers copy the collection, change the copy, and build a new template.
Run the tests until all thirteen pass.
hints: `require(condition) { "idempotency key is required" }` throws `IllegalArgumentException` with that message when the condition is false.
`LineItemsBuilder().apply(block).build()`: `apply` runs the lambda with the builder as `this` and returns the builder.
In a record's compact constructor, `tags = List.copyOf(tags);` reassigns the parameter before the field is set. You don't write `this.tags = ...`.

alt.title: Java

recap: Kotlin named and default arguments, plus `copy()`, replace most builders. Put validation in `init`: it runs for every construction, `copy()` included.
A builder still helps for Java callers, for construction spread over several steps, and for nested data. In Java, pair a validating record (compact constructor) with a builder that only collects.
A type-safe DSL is a function that takes a lambda with receiver (`Builder.() -> Unit`). `@DslMarker` stops an inner block from silently reaching an outer builder.
`Cloneable` has no `clone` method and `Object.clone()` is shallow. Use copy constructors, copy factories or withers.
Record withers and data class `copy()` are shallow. Store collections that can't change, and build new collections in withers.
In Kotlin 2.4 a private constructor doesn't make `copy()` private. Add `@ConsistentCopyVisibility`, or rely on `init` checks, which `copy()` runs.

quiz.q: `data class Fee(val bps: Int) { init { require(bps in 0..1_000) } }`. What does `Fee(290).copy(bps = 5_000)` do?
quiz.why: `copy()` calls the primary constructor with the new values, so every `init` block runs again and `require` throws. That's why `init` is the safest place for a data class's rules. What `copy()` does skip is a validating factory, when the constructor is private.

quiz.q: A Java team will call your Kotlin `ChargeRequest(amountMinor, currency, token, descriptor = null, capture = true, maxRetries = 0)` constructor from many places. What helps them most?
options: Add `@JvmOverloads`, or give them a builder
quiz.why: Java has no named or default arguments, so it sees one six-parameter constructor. `@JvmOverloads` generates overloads that drop trailing defaults, and a builder lets them set any subset by name. `@JvmStatic` applies to companion members, not constructors, and `data` changes nothing for Java callers here.

quiz.q: A DSL has no `@DslMarker`. Inside `lineItems { }`, someone writes `currency = "USD"`. `LineItemsBuilder` has no `currency`, but the outer `PaymentRequestBuilder` does. What happens?
quiz.why: Both receivers are in scope inside the inner lambda, so the compiler resolves `currency` on the outer builder and sets it. Nothing fails. With `@DslMarker` on both builders, that line becomes a compile error unless you write `this@paymentRequest.currency`.

quiz.q: `record Cart(String id, List<String> skus) {}`. `c1` was built with `new ArrayList<>(List.of("a"))`. Then `Cart c2 = new Cart("c2", c1.skus()); c2.skus().add("b");`. What happens?
options: `c1` is unchanged, because records are immutable
quiz.why: Records are only shallowly immutable: the field can't point elsewhere, but the `ArrayList` it points to can change, and `c2` shares it. A compact constructor with `skus = List.copyOf(skus);` would give each record its own unmodifiable list, and the `add` would then throw.

quiz.q: From *Factory Method and Abstract Factory*: you hide a data class's constructor (`data class Email private constructor(val value: String)`) and offer a validating `Email.of(raw)`. In Kotlin 2.4, which line still creates an unvalidated `Email`?
options: None: a private constructor covers every path
quiz.why: The generated `copy()` stays public even when the constructor is private; Kotlin 2.4 only warns about it. So `copy` creates an `Email` your factory never saw. `@ConsistentCopyVisibility` makes `copy()` private, and an `init` check would run on `copy()` too. A direct constructor call from outside does not compile.

flashcards.front: Does a Kotlin data class's `init` block run on `copy()`?
flashcards.back: Yes. `copy()` calls the primary constructor, so `require` checks in `init` run again.

flashcards.front: What is a lambda with receiver?
flashcards.back: A function type like `Builder.() -> Unit`. Inside the lambda, `this` is the Builder, so you call its members without a prefix.
Calling a member of an outer DSL receiver implicitly from inside an inner block. Reaching it then needs an explicit `this@label`.
It declares no `clone` method, and `Object.clone()` is protected, shallow and throws a checked exception. Use copy constructors or withers.

flashcards.front: Is a Kotlin data class `copy()` deep or shallow?
flashcards.back: Shallow. A property that holds a mutable object, such as a `MutableList`, is shared by the original and the copy.

flashcards.front: Where does validation go for a Java record that has a builder?
flashcards.back: In the record's compact constructor, so `build()`, withers and direct `new` calls all run it.

flashcards.front: `data class Email private constructor(...)`: is its `copy()` private in Kotlin 2.4?
flashcards.back: No. It stays public, with a warning. Add `@ConsistentCopyVisibility` to make it private.

terms.plain: A chain of constructors, each adding one more optional parameter.
A helper that collects values step by step and makes the finished object in `build()`.
A lambda whose `this` is a given object, written `T.() -> R`.
A meta-annotation for DSL marker annotations that limits implicit calls to the nearest receiver.
Making a new object by copying an existing one and changing a few fields.
A method like `withTimeout(t)` that returns a copy with one field changed.
A copy that shares the objects its fields point to, instead of copying them too.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague says: "Kotlin data classes are immutable, so `copy()` gives us safe, independent templates." Explain where that's wrong, and how you'd make templates safe in Kotlin and in Java.
explain_back.answer: Data classes are only as immutable as their properties. `val` stops a property from pointing somewhere else, but if it holds a `MutableList` or a `HashMap`, `copy()` copies the reference, so the template and every copy share that collection, and changing one changes all of them. To make templates safe, give them collections that can't change: in Kotlin, read-only `List` and `Map` types and `copy(items = items + x)` to build new ones; in Java, a record whose compact constructor stores `List.copyOf` and `Map.copyOf`, and withers that copy, change the copy and construct a new record. I'd also put the rules in `init` or the compact constructor, because `copy()` and withers go through them.

deeper.body:
Effective Java's hierarchical builder solves a problem you may meet in a shared Java library: a `Pizza.Builder` that subclasses (`NyPizza.Builder`, `Calzone.Builder`) extend without losing the subclass type in a chain. It uses a recursive type parameter, `Builder<T extends Builder<T>>`, and an abstract `self()` method that each subclass implements as `return this;`. *Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance* in the generics track showed why that recursive bound works. In Kotlin you almost never need it, because named arguments and `copy()` remove the chain.

Java has no `with` syntax for records yet. Project Amber has proposed one, derived record creation (JEP 468), where you would write something like `point with { x = 3; }`. Check its status on the JEP page before you plan around it. Until then, write withers for the fields that really change.

People sometimes deep-copy an object graph by serializing and deserializing it, or with a reflection library. It works, it is slow, and it copies things you didn't mean to copy, such as a shared `Clock` or a connection. If you need a deep copy, the cleaner fix is usually to make the components immutable so a shallow copy is enough.

Kotlin's `buildList { add(...) }`, `buildMap { }` and `buildString { }` are small standard-library builders with receivers. Use them when you build a collection with loops or conditions; the result is read-only once the block returns.
